content: Start with the default cube, give it a Geometry Nodes Modifier, and then set up the network with an [k]Ico Sphere[/k] and [k]Dual Mesh[/k] (Image 1). The [k]Dual Mesh[/k] node converts a mesh into its dual, i.e. faces are turned into vertices and vertices are turned into faces (Image 2). Using this node gives our sphere a better shape for our asteroid. Add in an [k]Extrude Mesh[/k] node and set the Offset very low (Image 3). The [k]Extrude Mesh[/k] node generates new edges or faces on the selected geometry elements and moves them by a certain offset. Add a [k]Scale Elements[/k] node, and make its selection the Top output of the [k]Extrude Mesh[/k] (Image 4).
The [i]Extrude Mesh Node[/i] generates new edges or faces on the selected geometry elements and moves them by a certain offset.

The operations are similar to the extrude tools in mesh edit mode, though there are some differences. Most importantly, the node never keeps the back-faces of the extrusion in place, they are always removed. Attribute propagation rules may also be different.
A boolean field indicating the “top” elements in the extrusion. In [i]Vertex[/i] mode, these are the new vertices; in [i]Edge[/i] mode, the new edges; and in [i]Face[/i] mode, the moved faces.

A boolean field indicating the “side” elements in the extrusion. In [i]Vertex[/i] mode, these are the new edges; in [i]Edge[/i] mode, the new faces; and in [i]Face[/i] mode, too, the newly generated faces (as opposed to the moved ones).

Add a [k]Scale Elements[/k] node, and make its selection the Top output of the [k]Extrude Mesh[/k] (Image 4). [k]Shift-D[/k] the [k]Extrude Mesh[/k] node and extrude after the scaling, but limit the extrusion just to the Top elements of the first extrusion (Image 5). Change the Offset Scale of the second [k]Extrude Mesh[/k] so that the faces extrude inwards (Image 6). Duplicate the [k]Scale Elements[/k] node and connect it to the network, using it to scale in the indentations we made (Image 7). Add in a [k]Subdivision Surface[/k] node, increase the Level, and add a [k]Set Shade Smooth[/k] node (Image 8).

We will start varying the shape by adding some [k]Random Value[/k] nodes. The first [k]Random Value[/k] node will be used to randomize the Offset Scale applied to the first [k]Extrude Mesh[/k] node and the second [k]Random Value[/k] node will randomize the scale applied to the Top faces (Image 9). Next, we will randomize how many sides get extruded into craters; add a [k]Random Value[/k] node, attach it to the Selection input for the first [k]Extrude Mesh[/k] node and adjust the [k]Random Value[/k]'s Min input to see some craters get removed (Image 10). You can also increase the Subdivisions for the [k]Ico Sphere[/k] node to give the surface more faces (Image 11). Define a material and set it with a [k]Set Material[/k] node (Image 12).

content: Start with the default cube, give it a Geometry Nodes Modifier, and then set up the network with an [k]Grid[/k] node (Image 1). Create a simple tile in the scene which we will scatter on the grid (Image 2). Hide the tile, bring it into the network, and add it to the scene with an [k]Instance on Points[/k] node (Image 3).

We want to alternate the tiles. Start by adding a [k]Mesh to Points[/k] node and change the Mode to Edges (Image 4). Change the Size X or Size Y of the [k]Grid[/k] node to 1/2 the other size, this will bring the tiles closer together (Image 5).

content: Start with the alternating tiles from the previous lesson, and change the Size X to 1 and the Size Y to 0.5 (Image 1). We will be changing the position, so add in a [k]Set Position[/k] node to do this, and a [k]Position[/k] node to read the position (Image 2). We will only be displacing the tiles on a single axis, so bring in a [k]Separate XYZ[/k] node and an [k]Add[/k] node to perform a math operation (Image 3). The full network will take the X value of the instance's position, add a floating point value to it, map it to a curve, multiply by a constant factor, then set it as the Z position of the instance (Image 4). To create a bridge shaped-curve, bring the far end of the curve down and bring up the middle (Image 5). Changing the Value in the [k]Multiply[/k] node will change the factor at which the curve is applied (Image 6). Set the [k]Add[/k] node to enable Clamp and then adjust the Value to see what it does (Image 7). You can also add another [k]Multiply[/k] node after the [k]Separate XYZ[/k] to tighten the curve (Image 8).
We can limit the effect to just a section of the mesh by limiting the changes by each instance's y-position. We can do that with the following network, adjusting the Threshold as needed (Image 9).

content: Normally we scatter objects like trees and rocks across a landscape with a [k]Distribute Points on Faces[/k] and an [k]Instance on Points[/k] node, but sometime that isn't optimal when we have vertical faces (Image 1). Let's use a [k]Normal[/k], [k]Separate XYZ[/k], [k]Map Range[/k], [k]Float Curve[/k] node to limit the points to those whose z-index of their normal is between a certain range, and then use a [k]Multiply[/k] node to increase the output, and plug that into the Density of the [k]Distribute Points on Faces[/k] (Image 2). Adjust the curve in the [k]Float Curve[/k] node to adjust how many instances appear in the flatter vs. more sloped parts of the mesh (Image 3).

Start the network with an [k]Ico Sphere[/k], a [k]Subdivision Surface[/k], and a [k]Set to Shade Smooth[/k] (Image 1). Apply noise as a displacement effect with a [k]Noise Texture[/k], [k]Normal[/k], [k]Multiply (Vector)[/k], and [k]Set Position[/k] node (Image 2). Duplicate the [k]Subdivision Surface[/k] node and add it towards the end of the network to smooth things out again (Image 3). We want to make it more intense, but adjusting the noise values just makes the sphere more distorted beyond just the surface. We need o remap the noise values. Noise textures have a range from 0.0 to 1.0, while Normal values are between -1.0 and 1.0. Add a [k]Map Range (Vector)[/k] node to re-map the To Min noise values from -1.0 to 1.0 (Image 4). Add another [k]Multiply (Vector)[/k] node and a constant [k]Value[/k] and adjusting the Value and the Noise levels will give us greater control (Image 5).

content: Start the network with a [k]Grid[/k] and an [k]Extrude Mesh[/k] node (Image 1). Add a [k]Scale Elements[/k] node and set the Scale in both nodes to 0.0 and the Selection to the Top Faces (Image 2). Add in a [k]Merge by Distance[/k] and a [k]Dual Mesh[/k] and see the pattern change to octagons (Image 3). Enabling Keep Boundaries on the [k]Dual Mesh[/k] node will fix the sides (Image 4).

Start over with a [k]Grid[/k] and a [k]Triangulate[/k] node (Image 5). Add a [k]Transform Geometry[k] node to rotate it 45 degrees in the z-axis and another one to scale 0.66666 in the x-axis (Image 6).

We can mask part of our mesh with another mesh. Using the previous grid pattern, add a Cube to the scene and bring it into the network (Image 1). Bring in a [k]Bounding Box[/k] node to read the cube's boundaries, and a [k]Position[/k] and [/k]Absolute (Vector)[/k] node to convert negative position values to positive ones (Image 2). Add a [k]Subtract (Vector)[/k] node to subtract the Max value of the [k]Bounding Box[/k] from the absolute position (Image 3). Separate the axes with a [k]Separate XYZ[/k] node and feed the X and Y outputs into an [k]Or[/k] node (Image 4). Bring in a [k]Delete Geometry[/k] node with its Domain set to Face before the output and set its Selection input to the Boolean output (Image 5)

content: Add a Bézier Curve to the scene and straighten it out (Image 1). Add a Geometry Nodes Modifier to it, and give it a [k]Resample Curve[/k] node with the Mode set to Length and the Length to 0.35m (Image 2). This will break the curve up into points that are all equal distance from each other, based on the Length you set. Create a quick low poly fence post (Image 3). Hide the post, move it to the network and instance it on the curve (Image 4). In Edit Mode, if you grab any of the curve vertices and move them, the fence instances will follow (Image 5). We will make this a double fence by duplicating the instances and sending both to the output (Image 6). We want to add separation, so give each set of instances their own [k]Transform Geometry[/k] node and separate them on the y-axis and move one on the x-axis to offset (Image 7). Let's add posts to the ends of the fence. Instance a cube, scale it to the right size and then use an [k]Endpoint Selection[/k] node to set it so only the first and last point on the curve get a post (Image 8). Adjust the scale on the fence posts so that there is better spacing between posts (Image 9). We need to remove any fence posts that are outside of our first and last cubes; add an [k]Endpoint Selection[/k] and subtract one from the output value with a [k]Subtract[/k] node and feed that into the Selection input for the [k]Instance on Points[/k] node (Image 10).

Let's add some rails to the fence. Bring in a [k]Curve to Mesh[/k] node to read the original geometry and a [k]Quadrilateral[/k] as its profile shape (Image 11). Scale the rail down and move it up with a [k]Transform Geometry[/k] node (Image 12). Add two more transforms for rails at the top and middle (Image 13).

Add a [k]Curve Tangent[/k] node and a [k]Align Euler to Vector[/k] node and connect them to the rotation for all [k]Instance on Points[/k] nodes (Image 14). Now as we move the fence around it will grow and follow the curve (Image 15).
